conflicts.description: The same broad person/performer concept is named name in IMDb and actor in Sakila, with different identifier and name-column conventions.
conflicts.resolution: A unified person resource was created. Source identifiers feed person_id, while IMDb display_name remains distinct from Sakila's atomic first_name and last_name because they are not semantically interchangeable.

conflicts.description: Audiovisual works are called titles in IMDb and films in Sakila; title columns also use primarytitle versus title.
conflicts.resolution: The entities were unified as work, and equivalent display-title values were named primary_title.

conflicts.description: IMDb calls work classifications genres while Sakila calls them categories.
conflicts.resolution: Both are represented by neutral classification and work_classification resources.

conflicts.description: Equivalent duration attributes use different names.
conflicts.resolution: They were unified as runtime_seconds.

conflicts.description: IMDb alphanumeric identifiers are incorrectly declared as number in several source resources despite descriptions specifying strings.
conflicts.resolution: All alphanumeric IMDb identifiers are represented as string.

conflicts.description: IMDb primarytitle is declared integer although its description defines textual content.
conflicts.resolution: primary_title is typed string.

conflicts.description: Calendar years are represented as strings in the sources.
conflicts.resolution: Valid years are typed integer, with source null sentinels treated as missing values.

conflicts.description: Durations and monetary amounts are declared as strings.
conflicts.resolution: Durations are numeric integer seconds and monetary values are number, without inventing an unavailable currency.

conflicts.description: Boolean status flags are encoded as strings.
conflicts.resolution: The target uses boolean is_active fields.

conflicts.description: Source fields described as date-and-time values are typed date.
conflicts.resolution: The target uses datetime for event timestamps.

conflicts.description: Foreign-key columns use integer while their referenced source primary keys are declared string.
conflicts.resolution: Target foreign and primary key types are consistently string.

conflicts.description: Runtime is stored in minutes rather than the target's standard physical unit.
conflicts.resolution: Runtime is standardized to SI seconds.

conflicts.description: Rental duration is expressed in days.
conflicts.resolution: Rental duration is standardized to SI seconds.

conflicts.description: IMDb average user rating is a numeric preference score, while Sakila rating is a categorical audience content classification.
conflicts.resolution: The semantically distinct values remain separate as average_user_rating and content_rating.

conflicts.description: IMDb alias language is a free code or label, whereas Sakila uses a keyed language entity for a film's language.
conflicts.resolution: Alias language remains language_code on work_alias; Sakila film language relationships use language_id and are not conflated.

conflicts.description: IMDb supplies a credited display name, while Sakila separates legal-style given and family names.
conflicts.resolution: display_name, first_name, and last_name remain distinct to avoid asserting equivalence between different name semantics.

conflicts.description: IMDb startyear can mean series start year, while Sakila release_year is a film release year.
conflicts.resolution: The unified attribute is explicitly named release_start_year to preserve the shared inception-year meaning without implying every work is a film.

conflicts.description: Multiple source columns contain arrays or multi-value content inside scalar strings.
conflicts.resolution: Values were atomized into person_profession, person_known_work, work_classification, work_alias_type, work_alias_attribute, work_credit, and work_special_feature rows.

conflicts.description: Credits are decomposed differently: IMDb has principal-credit rows plus director/writer arrays, while Sakila has a film-actor bridge.
conflicts.resolution: All are normalized into work_credit with foreign keys to work and person and optional role-specific attributes.

conflicts.description: Sakila duplicates title and description in a separate full-text support table.
conflicts.resolution: Semantically identical film_text attributes are merged into work rather than preserving a duplicate entity.

conflicts.description: A point geometry is carried as one non-generic composite string.
conflicts.resolution: It is split into atomic numeric latitude and longitude fields compatible with generic Frictionless types.

conflicts.description: Episode hierarchy is stored as a relationship table separate from title basics.
conflicts.resolution: A normalized episode subtype/relationship resource references work twice, once for the episode and once for its parent.

conflicts.description: IMDb embeds up to three genres in each title row, while Sakila models a many-to-many film-category relationship.
conflicts.resolution: Both are represented as the N:M work_classification bridge.

conflicts.description: IMDb embeds a one-to-many list of known works in each person row.
conflicts.resolution: The list is represented as person_known_work, allowing multiple works per person and multiple people per work.

conflicts.description: Contributor relationships vary between arrays, ordered principal rows, and an explicit many-to-many actor bridge.
conflicts.resolution: A row-per-person-per-credit representation is used in work_credit; repeated characters can produce separate atomic credit rows.

conflicts.description: Each alias can have multiple types and multiple descriptive attributes.
conflicts.resolution: Separate one-to-many child resources preserve each atomic type and attribute.

conflicts.description: Ratings are conceptually optional one-to-one data for a work but are stored in a separate resource without an explicit primary key.
conflicts.resolution: work_rating uses work_id as its primary key and foreign key, enforcing at most one aggregate rating row per work.

conflicts.description: Unified people have incompatible source key domains: IMDb natural-style alphanumeric identifiers and Sakila surrogate actor identifiers.
conflicts.resolution: Both source primary keys map to string person_id, with source-system identity retained during integration to prevent collisions.

conflicts.description: Unified works use different source identifiers and key styles.
conflicts.resolution: Both primary keys map to string work_id, with source-system identity retained during integration.

conflicts.description: title_akas has no declared primary key although ordering is documented as unique within a title.
conflicts.resolution: work_alias uses the composite key work_id plus alias_order.

conflicts.description: title_episode has no declared primary key even though each episode work has one parent-series relationship.
conflicts.resolution: episode_work_id is the primary key and also a foreign key to work.

conflicts.description: title_ratings lacks a declared primary key despite containing one aggregate row per title.
conflicts.resolution: work_id is used as the work_rating primary key.

conflicts.description: payment has no declared primary key although payment_id is described as its unique surrogate identifier.
conflicts.resolution: payment_id is promoted to the required target primary key.

conflicts.description: Sakila bridge tables declare foreign keys but no primary keys.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized bridges use relationship-based keys where the relationship is unique; work_credit instead uses a synthetic credit_id because richer IMDb credits can repeat a work-person pair.

conflicts.description: Store and staff form a cyclic foreign-key dependency.
conflicts.resolution: Both relationships are retained because they represent different semantics: a store's manager and a staff member's home store.

conflicts.description: The same broad media-work concept is named title in IMDb and film in Sakila, with different identifier names.
conflicts.resolution: Unified the concepts under media_title with a canonical source-qualified media_title_id.

conflicts.description: IMDb calls the entity a name/person while Sakila models the overlapping acting subset as actor.
conflicts.resolution: Unified both under person while retaining source-specific name representations.

conflicts.description: IMDb uses genre terminology while Sakila uses category for media classification.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized the classification entity as category and its label as category_name.

conflicts.description: Equivalent duration attributes use different names.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized the attribute as runtime_seconds.

conflicts.description: The source table name inventory can denote either a collection or an individual copy.
conflicts.resolution: Renamed the row-level entity to inventory_item and its key to inventory_item_id.

conflicts.description: IMDb alphanumeric identifiers are incorrectly declared as number despite descriptions specifying strings.
conflicts.resolution: Typed all canonical IMDb-derived identifiers as string.

conflicts.description: The primary title is declared integer but described as text.
conflicts.resolution: Typed primary_title as string.

conflicts.description: Year values are represented as strings and may contain source null markers.
conflicts.resolution: Typed valid normalized years as integer and treated source null markers as missing values.

conflicts.description: Numeric durations and monetary amounts are represented as strings.
conflicts.resolution: Typed durations and amounts as number after normalization.

conflicts.description: Boolean status values are represented as strings.
conflicts.resolution: Typed normalized activity indicators as boolean.

conflicts.description: Fields declared as date are described or conventionally used as timestamps.
conflicts.resolution: Used datetime where time-of-day semantics are present or updates are timestamp-like.

conflicts.description: Foreign-key types differ from the string types of their referenced source primary keys.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized target foreign keys to string to match their target primary keys.

conflicts.description: Runtime is recorded in minutes rather than a standard SI unit.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized runtime to seconds in runtime_seconds.

conflicts.description: Rental duration is recorded in days.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized rental duration to seconds in rental_duration_seconds.

conflicts.description: The word rating is a homonym: IMDb stores an aggregate user score while Sakila stores an audience classification code.
conflicts.resolution: Kept the concepts separate as average_user_rating and content_rating_code.

conflicts.description: IMDb provides a language code on an alternative title while Sakila uses a surrogate language key and English language name.
conflicts.resolution: Preserved IMDb's value as language_code on alternative_title and retained Sakila's normalized language entity, avoiding an unsupported equivalence.

conflicts.description: Monetary amounts have no explicit source currency.
conflicts.resolution: Retained numeric amounts without asserting a currency.

conflicts.description: A geometry value contains multiple spatial coordinates in a non-generic source type.
conflicts.resolution: Represented it atomically as numeric latitude_degrees and longitude_degrees.

conflicts.description: Multiple source columns encode arrays inside scalar strings.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized repeating values into profession, known-title, category, alternative-title type/attribute, title-credit, character, and special-feature child or bridge resources.

conflicts.description: Sakila duplicates searchable film text in a separate film_text table.
conflicts.resolution: Merged semantically identical title and description attributes into media_title with combined provenance.

conflicts.description: Episode hierarchy is stored in a relationship table rather than directly on title rows.
conflicts.resolution: Retained a normalized episode relationship resource with two distinct foreign keys to media_title.

conflicts.description: The address geometry is composite and not supported by the permitted generic target types.
conflicts.resolution: Decomposed it into atomic latitude and longitude fields.

conflicts.description: IMDb embeds up to three title genres while Sakila models film-category as an explicit many-to-many relationship.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized both as the title_category bridge.

conflicts.description: Title-person participation is represented by embedded lists, detailed principal rows, and a many-to-many actor bridge.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized participation as title_credit rows, with normalized character rows and role indicators.

conflicts.description: Known-for titles are a multi-valued person-to-title association embedded in one column.
conflicts.resolution: Materialized person_known_title as a many-to-many bridge.

conflicts.description: A title can have multiple localized alternative-title rows distinguished only by per-title ordering.
conflicts.resolution: Modeled alternative_title as a one-to-many child entity with its own synthetic row identifier.

conflicts.description: A film can have many physical inventory copies and each copy belongs to one store.
conflicts.resolution: Preserved inventory_item as a distinct child entity between media titles and rentals.

conflicts.description: Equivalent media entities use natural alphanumeric and surrogate numeric key domains that can collide when represented as strings.
conflicts.resolution: Defined a canonical source-qualified media_title_id while preserving all corresponding source key provenance.

conflicts.description: Equivalent person entities use unrelated identifier domains.
conflicts.resolution: Defined a canonical source-qualified person_id with both source primary keys in provenance.

conflicts.description: Ordering values are only unique within a parent title and are not declared source primary keys.
conflicts.resolution: Introduced synthetic identifiers for alternative-title and title-credit rows while retaining ordering as a source attribute.

conflicts.description: Episode and rating tables omit declared primary keys even though each row is functionally identified by its title.
conflicts.resolution: Used episode_title_id and media_title_id respectively as target primary keys.

conflicts.description: Payment has a documented unique surrogate identifier but no declared source primary key.
conflicts.resolution: Promoted payment_id to the target primary key.

conflicts.description: Source bridge tables omit composite primary keys.
conflicts.resolution: Applied composite keys to deterministic bridges and a synthetic key where heterogeneous credit structures require one normalized row identity.

conflicts.description: Divergent field naming for person identifiers across sources (IMDB uses 'nconst' string ID, Sakila uses separate surrogate keys for different person types).
conflicts.resolution: Unified into a single 'person_id' string field in the 'person' table, accommodating all source identifier formats.

conflicts.description: Inconsistent naming for media title identifiers (IMDB 'tconst' vs Sakila 'film_id').
conflicts.resolution: Standardized as 'media_id' in the 'media_title' table, with string type to handle both alphanumeric and numeric string formats.

conflicts.description: Different field names for the primary display title of media items.
conflicts.resolution: Consolidated into 'primary_title' field in 'media_title' table, preserving semantic equivalence.

conflicts.description: Naming discrepancy for release year attributes.
conflicts.resolution: Mapped to 'release_year' in 'media_title' with integer type for consistent sorting.

conflicts.description: Inconsistent naming for runtime duration fields.
conflicts.resolution: Unified as 'runtime_minutes' with integer type, converting Sakila's string-based length to numeric.

conflicts.description: Genre representation uses different naming conventions (array field vs category table).
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into 'genre' and 'media_genre' tables, with genre names sourced from both schemas.

conflicts.description: Fragmented and inconsistent naming for person-media relationships across crew/actor tables.
conflicts.resolution: Centralized in 'media_person' table with explicit role categorization, preserving all source mappings.

conflicts.description: IMDB incorrectly defines alphanumeric identifiers (nconst, tconst) as 'number' type in schema, while they are actually string values.
conflicts.resolution: Corrected to 'string' type in target schema to accurately represent the data format.

conflicts.description: Year fields are stored as strings in IMDB, preventing proper numeric operations and sorting.
conflicts.resolution: Converted to 'integer' type in target schema for consistent numeric handling.

conflicts.description: IMDB schema incorrectly specifies 'primarytitle' as 'integer' type, but it represents textual title data.
conflicts.resolution: Fixed to 'string' type in 'media_title' table.

conflicts.description: Type mismatch between IMDB's integer runtime and Sakila's string-based length field.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized as 'integer' in target, with IMDB value used directly and Sakila value converted during integration.

conflicts.description: Multiple numeric fields in Sakila are stored as strings, impeding mathematical operations.
conflicts.resolution: Converted to appropriate numeric types ('integer' for durations, 'number' for monetary values) in target schema.

conflicts.description: Fundamentally different rating systems: IMDB uses a 1-10 numeric scale for user ratings, while Sakila uses categorical MPAA ratings (G, PG-13, etc.).
conflicts.resolution: Separated into distinct rating systems in 'media_rating' table with a 'rating_system' discriminator field to maintain semantic distinction.

conflicts.description: IMDB includes an adult content flag with no direct equivalent in Sakila's schema.
conflicts.resolution: Preserved as 'is_adult' boolean in 'media_title' table, with null values for Sakila-sourced records.

conflicts.description: IMDB stores genres as a comma-separated array within a single field, while Sakila uses a normalized category table with explicit relationships.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into dedicated 'genre' and 'media_genre' tables, splitting the array into atomic values.

conflicts.description: IMDB uses array fields for multiple type/attribute values on alternative titles, violating atomicity.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into separate 'media_alternative_title_type' and 'media_alternative_title_attribute' tables to maintain atomic values.

conflicts.description: IMDB stores multiple directors/writers as arrays within single fields, losing individual role granularity.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into 'media_person' table with explicit role categorization for each individual.

conflicts.description: IMDB heavily uses denormalized array/composite fields for multi-valued attributes, while Sakila employs normalized junction tables.
conflicts.resolution: All multi-valued attributes were decomposed into atomic fields across dedicated tables (e.g., 'person_known_for', 'person_profession', 'media_genre').

conflicts.description: Sakila maintains separate tables for different person types (actors, staff, customers), whereas IMDB uses a single unified 'name_basics' table.
conflicts.resolution: Consolidated into a single 'person' table with role-specific relationships captured in other tables (e.g., 'media_person' for media roles).

conflicts.description: IMDB explicitly models TV series episode hierarchies (parent series to episode relationships), which has no structural equivalent in Sakila.
conflicts.resolution: Preserved in 'media_episode' table with foreign keys to 'media_title' for both parent series and individual episodes.

conflicts.description: IMDB's array fields (directors, writers) imply a one-to-many relationship within a single row, while Sakila's 'film_actor' table explicitly models a many-to-many relationship via junction table.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized to many-to-many via 'media_person' table, which can represent all role types (directors, writers, actors) with consistent cardinality.

conflicts.description: IMDB uses alphanumeric string identifiers (stored as numbers in schema) while Sakila uses numeric string surrogates for different entity types.
conflicts.resolution: Unified all entity identifiers as 'string' type in target schema, with 'person_id' serving as the primary key for the 'person' table.

conflicts.description: Several IMDB tables lack explicit primary key definitions in their schema, with some relying on composite keys not formally declared.
conflicts.resolution: Added surrogate primary keys where necessary (e.g., 'alternative_title_id' for 'media_alternative_title') or formally declared composite keys (e.g., ['media_id', 'genre_id'] for 'media_genre').

conflicts.description: Person identifiers use different naming conventions: IMDb uses 'nconst' (alphanumeric natural key) while Sakila uses separate surrogate keys ('actor_id', 'staff_id', 'customer_id').

conflicts.description: Work identifiers: IMDb 'tconst' vs Sakila 'film_id'.
conflicts.resolution: Unified as 'work_id' in 'work' table with string type.

conflicts.description: Primary title field: IMDb 'primarytitle' (mis-typed as integer) vs Sakila 'title'.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized as 'title' in 'work' with string type, correcting IMDb's type error.

conflicts.description: Release year synonyms: 'startyear' vs 'release_year'.
conflicts.resolution: Mapped to 'release_year' in 'work' with integer type.

conflicts.description: Runtime field: 'runtimeminutes' vs 'length'.
conflicts.resolution: Unified as 'runtime_minutes' in 'work' with integer type (SI unit).

conflicts.description: Genre representation: string array vs normalized table.
conflicts.resolution: Created 'genre' and 'work_genre' tables to normalize both.

conflicts.description: Language: field in title_akas vs separate table.

conflicts.description: IMDb defines nconst/tconst as 'number' but they are alphanumeric strings.

conflicts.description: IMDb's primarytitle is typed as integer but is string.
conflicts.resolution: Corrected to string type.

conflicts.description: Year fields stored as strings but represent integers.
conflicts.resolution: Converted to integer type.

conflicts.description: Numeric values stored as strings in Sakila.
conflicts.resolution: Converted to number/integer types.

conflicts.description: IMDb stores multi-valued data in single columns as arrays/strings.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into dedicated tables (person_known_for_work, person_profession, etc.).

conflicts.description: IMDb free-form genres vs Sakila controlled vocabulary, but values overlap.
conflicts.resolution: Mapped to unified 'genre' table.

conflicts.description: Language names from both schemas represent the same semantic concept.
conflicts.resolution: Unified in 'language' table.

conflicts.description: IMDb: single person table vs Sakila: separate tables for actors/staff/customers.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into 'person' table with 'person_type' discriminator.

conflicts.description: IMDb supports TV series episodes; Sakila is movie-only.
conflicts.resolution: Created 'work' table with 'work_type', and 'work_episode' for series data.

conflicts.description: IMDb: arrays in title_crew vs Sakila: normalized film_actor table.
conflicts.resolution: Created 'person_work_role' table for all roles.

conflicts.description: IMDb: genres as string array vs Sakila: normalized film_category.
conflicts.resolution: Created 'genre' and 'work_genre' tables.

conflicts.description: IMDb: language in title_akas vs Sakila: separate language table.
conflicts.resolution: Unified language handling in 'language' and 'work_language' tables.

conflicts.description: Arrays in title_crew imply 1:N but denormalized.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized to M:N via 'person_work_role' with role_type.

conflicts.description: Array in name_basics implies 1:N but denormalized.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized to M:N via 'person_known_for_work'.

conflicts.description: IMDb: natural keys vs Sakila: surrogate keys for persons.
conflicts.resolution: Unified as string 'person_id' with 'person_type' context.

conflicts.description: IMDb's title_akas lacks primary key.
conflicts.resolution: Added synthetic 'alternative_title_id'.

conflicts.description: Multiple IMDb tables lack primary keys.
conflicts.resolution: Added synthetic primary keys where needed.

conflicts.description: Different field names for the primary identifier of media content entities (tconst vs film_id). Both represent the same semantic concept of a unique work identifier but use different naming conventions.
conflicts.resolution: Unified under a surrogate work_id in the work table, with source-specific identifier fields (imdb_tconst, sakila_film_id) to preserve original identifiers. This maintains semantic homogeneity while resolving naming discrepancies.

conflicts.description: Inconsistent naming for person identifiers across sources (nconst for IMDb, actor_id/staff_id for Sakila). All represent unique person identifiers but with different prefixes and schemas.
conflicts.resolution: Consolidated into a unified person table with a surrogate person_id. Source-specific identifiers are stored as separate attributes (imdb_nconst, sakila_actor_id, sakila_staff_id) to preserve lineage and avoid semantic merging of distinct identifier systems.

conflicts.description: Different field names for the primary title of a work (primarytitle vs title), despite representing the same semantic attribute.
conflicts.resolution: Mapped both to a canonical title field in the work table. The semantic equivalence of 'primary title' and 'title' justifies this unification under a single field.

conflicts.description: Genre information is named differently and structured differently (genres as an array field vs category as a separate table with a name field).
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into a dedicated genre table with a name field, allowing both sources to contribute to the same semantic entity. The array structure in IMDb is resolved via the work_genre bridge table.

conflicts.description: Alphanumeric identifiers inconsistently typed as number (IMDb) or string (Sakila) in source schemas, despite being non-numeric in practice (e.g., 'nm0000001' for nconst).
conflicts.resolution: Standardized all identifier fields to string type in the target schema to accurately represent their alphanumeric nature. This resolves type mismatches while preserving data integrity.

conflicts.description: Year fields stored as string in IMDb (e.g., '1990'), but semantically represent integer years. Sakila uses string for release_year but with similar intent.
conflicts.resolution: Converted to integer type in the target schema (e.g., birth_year). This enforces atomicity and standardizes year representation as numeric values.

conflicts.description: Runtime stored as string in Sakila (e.g., '120') but represents an integer number of minutes.
conflicts.resolution: Mapped to runtime_minutes as integer in the work table, aligning with IMDb's integer runtimeminutes field. This ensures consistent typing for the same semantic attribute.

conflicts.description: Monetary amount stored as string in Sakila (e.g., '5.99'), but requires numeric operations.
conflicts.resolution: Converted to number type in the target schema to support arithmetic operations and consistent representation.

conflicts.description: Boolean flags stored as string ('true'/'false' or '1'/'0') in Sakila, despite representing binary states.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized to boolean type in the target schema (e.g., active field in customer and person tables). This resolves the type mismatch while preserving the semantic meaning.

conflicts.description: Primary title field incorrectly typed as integer in IMDb schema, but described as a string in the documentation.
conflicts.resolution: Corrected to string type in the target schema to match the semantic intent and actual data format.

conflicts.description: Fundamentally different rating systems: IMDb uses a numerical weighted average (0-10 scale), while Sakila uses categorical ratings (G, PG, PG-13, R, NC-17). These represent distinct semantic scales and cannot be merged.
conflicts.resolution: Preserved as separate fields in the work table (imdb_average_rating and sakila_rating). This maintains semantic integrity by acknowledging the incompatibility of the two systems.

conflicts.description: Runtime is measured in minutes in both sources, but Sakila's length is stored as a string. The semantic unit (minutes) is consistent, but representation differs.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into a single runtime_minutes field as integer. The common unit (minutes) and semantic meaning justify this merge, with type normalization to integer.

conflicts.description: Language representation differs: IMDb has language per alternative title (e.g., 'en'), while Sakila has a dedicated language table with names (e.g., 'English'). The semantic meaning (language of content) is the same, but granularity varies.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into a single language table with a name field. IMDb's language codes are mapped to this table, allowing both sources to contribute to the same semantic entity.

conflicts.description: Genres are stored as a comma-separated/array field in IMDb (denormalized), while Sakila uses a normalized structure with a category table and film_category bridge table.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into a dedicated genre table and work_genre bridge table. This resolves the structural discrepancy by applying a consistent normalized form to both sources.

conflicts.description: Multi-value attributes (attributes and types) are stored as arrays within single string fields in IMDb, violating atomicity.
conflicts.resolution: Split into atomic components via dedicated bridge tables (work_aka_attribute and work_aka_type). Each array element becomes a separate row, enforcing atomicity.

conflicts.description: Multiple person references (for directors and writers) are stored as arrays in single fields, creating a nested structure that is not normalized.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into the work_person bridge table. Each array element (nconst) is expanded into a separate row with the appropriate role (director/writer), resolving the nested structure.

conflicts.description: Array of work references (tconsts) stored in a single field, representing a many-to-many relationship between persons and works.
conflicts.resolution: Split into a dedicated person_known_for bridge table, where each tconst becomes a separate row linking a person to a work. This normalizes the many-to-many relationship.

conflicts.description: Array of profession strings stored in a single field, representing a one-to-many relationship between persons and professions.
conflicts.resolution: Split into a person_profession table, with one row per profession per person. This enforces atomicity and normalizes the data structure.

conflicts.description: Different cardinality handling for work-person relationships: IMDb uses arrays within title_crew (many directors/writers per work), while Sakila uses a bridge table (film_actor) for many actors per film. Both represent many-to-many relationships but with different structural implementations.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into a single work_person bridge table with a surrogate key. This consistently models the many-to-many relationship across both sources, accommodating all role types (actor, director, writer, etc.).

conflicts.description: Hierarchical relationship between TV series and episodes is implicit in IMDb: title_episode has parenttconst (series) and tconst (episode), while title_basics contains both series and episodes without explicit hierarchy.
conflicts.resolution: Explicitly modeled in the work table via parent_work_id (self-referencing foreign key), season_number, and episode_number fields. This standardizes the hierarchical structure for all work types.

conflicts.description: Different primary key strategies for person entities: IMDb uses natural keys (nconst), while Sakila uses surrogate keys (actor_id). This creates a conflict in how entities are uniquely identified.
conflicts.resolution: Introduced a surrogate person_id as the primary key in the unified person table. Source-specific identifiers (nconst, actor_id) are stored as non-key attributes to preserve their provenance and avoid merging distinct identifier systems.

conflicts.description: Different primary key systems for work entities: IMDb uses natural alphanumeric keys (tconst), while Sakila uses surrogate keys (film_id).
conflicts.resolution: Introduced a surrogate work_id as the primary key in the work table. Source-specific identifiers are retained as attributes (imdb_tconst, sakila_film_id) to maintain traceability to source systems.

conflicts.description: Primary key identification differs: IMDb explicitly defines primaryKey for title_basics (tconst), while Sakila's film table has an implicit primaryKey (film_id) not stated in the schema metadata but used in foreign keys.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized primary key handling by explicitly defining surrogate keys (work_id) in the target schema, with source-specific keys stored as attributes. This ensures consistent key management across the unified schema.

conflicts.description: The same movie/title entity is named title_basics in the IMDB schema and film in the Sakila schema; film_text is a denormalized duplicate of the same concept.
conflicts.resolution: Merged under a single resource named title, absorbing film_text as a denormalized duplicate.

conflicts.description: The same person entity is called name_basics in IMDB and actor in Sakila.
conflicts.resolution: Merged under a single resource named person.

conflicts.description: Title identifiers (tconst vs film_id) and person identifiers (nconst vs actor_id) use different column names for the same identity.
conflicts.resolution: Renamed to neutral title_id and person_id respectively.

conflicts.description: Equivalent attributes carry divergent names across schemas (startyear/release_year, runtimeminutes/length, primarytitle/title).
conflicts.resolution: Standardized to release_year, runtime_minutes and primary_title.

conflicts.description: The film classification taxonomy is named category in Sakila and genres in IMDB.
conflicts.resolution: Unified as genre with a shared name attribute.

conflicts.description: The token rating is a homonym: in IMDB it denotes a numeric user score, in Sakila it denotes an MPAA-style content rating.
conflicts.resolution: Disambiguated into separate attributes average_rating (numeric score) and content_rating (age/classification rating).

conflicts.description: IMDB models identifiers as number while Sakila models them as string (and some Sakila FK columns as integer).
conflicts.resolution: All identifiers standardized to string, since IMDB identifiers are alphanumeric and references must match.

conflicts.description: Runtime is typed as string in film.length but integer in title_basics.runtimeminutes.
conflicts.resolution: Cast to integer runtime_minutes (values expressed in minutes).

conflicts.description: All year attributes are typed as string in the sources, using a null sentinel for missing values.
conflicts.resolution: Converted to integer, mapping the null sentinel to null.

conflicts.description: Boolean flags are represented as string in the sources.
conflicts.resolution: Converted to boolean.

conflicts.description: Monetary values are typed as string in the sources.
conflicts.resolution: Converted to number.

conflicts.description: Date-time values are typed as date despite descriptions stating date and time.
conflicts.resolution: Typed as datetime to preserve the time component; pure date columns (last_update, create_date) remain date.

conflicts.description: title_basics.primarytitle is typed as integer although it holds textual title content.
conflicts.resolution: Corrected to string.

conflicts.description: Boolean attributes are documented as 0/1 integer codes.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized to boolean.

conflicts.description: Language is encoded as an ISO code in title_akas.language but as an English name in sakila.language.name; different encodings of the same dimension.
conflicts.resolution: Sakila retains language_id/name as the canonical language dimension; the IMDB alias language is kept as a distinct language_code attribute to avoid conflating code and name.

conflicts.description: The two genre/category taxonomies use overlapping but non-identical value sets (e.g. IMDB Drama vs Sakila Classics).
conflicts.resolution: Merged into a single genre dimension matched by name, accepting that the combined value space is broader than either source.

conflicts.description: Boolean semantics are encoded inconsistently (0/1 integers vs TRUE/FALSE strings).
conflicts.resolution: Standardized to a single boolean representation with true/false semantics.

conflicts.description: Both measure duration; IMDB uses an explicit minutes unit in the name, Sakila an implicit one.
conflicts.resolution: Kept as runtime_minutes with an explicit, consistent minutes unit.

conflicts.description: Missing values are encoded with a string sentinel in the IMDB year columns.
conflicts.resolution: Sentinel values reinterpreted as null in numeric target columns.

conflicts.description: Person-title involvement is modeled three different ways: multi-valued arrays (title_crew.directors/writers), an attributed credit table (title_principals with category/job/characters), and a plain junction table (film_actor).
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into a single title_credit resource capturing person, title, role, job and characters; crew arrays are exploded into one row per person with a fixed role.

conflicts.description: Genres are a multi-valued column in IMDB but a fully normalized many-to-many structure in Sakila.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into genre plus a title_genre junction table.

conflicts.description: A person notable titles are stored as an array of title identifiers.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into the person_known_for_title junction table.

conflicts.description: A person professions are stored as an array of strings.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into the person_profession child table.

conflicts.description: film_text denormalizes film title and description into a separate search table.
conflicts.resolution: Folded into the title resource; the duplicate columns were mapped onto the same target attributes.

conflicts.description: Episode relationships and ratings are held in separate 1:1 side tables in IMDB rather than embedded attributes.
conflicts.resolution: Preserved as dedicated title_episode and title_rating resources to keep the title entity normalized.

conflicts.description: Person names are stored as a single unsplit string in IMDB but split into first/last components in Sakila.
conflicts.resolution: Retained both representations (primary_name and first_name/last_name) to preserve information from either source.

conflicts.description: Title-to-genre is N:M in Sakila (junction table) but an unbounded multi-value field in IMDB.
conflicts.resolution: Modeled as an N:M relationship via the title_genre junction table.

conflicts.description: Person-to-title involvement is N:M across all sources.
conflicts.resolution: Modeled as an N:M relationship via the title_credit table.

conflicts.description: A title has many alternative titles (1:N).
conflicts.resolution: Preserved as a 1:N child resource title_aka keyed by (title_id, ordering).

conflicts.description: A TV series has many episodes (1:N self-referencing relationship).
conflicts.resolution: Preserved via title_episode with title_id and parent_title_id both referencing title.

conflicts.description: Ratings relate to a title 1:1.
conflicts.resolution: Kept as a 1:1 side table title_rating keyed by title_id.

conflicts.description: Persons and their known-for titles form an N:M relationship.
conflicts.resolution: Modeled as N:M via person_known_for_title.

conflicts.description: title_akas declares no primary key, though (titleid, ordering) uniquely identifies rows.
conflicts.resolution: Composite primary key defined as (title_id, ordering).

conflicts.description: Several source resources declare no primary key, leaving their identity ambiguous.
conflicts.resolution: Natural/composite keys were assigned where derivable (title_episode.title_id, title_rating.title_id, title_genre composite, title_aka composite) and a synthetic surrogate credit_id was introduced for title_credit.

conflicts.description: IMDB uses a natural alphanumeric key (tconst) while Sakila uses a surrogate key (film_id) for the same title entity.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into title_id whose provenance lists both source keys.

conflicts.description: IMDB uses a natural key (nconst) while Sakila uses a surrogate key (actor_id) for the same person entity.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into person_id whose provenance lists both source keys.

conflicts.description: film_text.film_id is a de facto foreign key to film but no foreign key is declared.
conflicts.resolution: Treated as an alias of the title identifier and folded into title_id.

conflicts.description: The person entity is named 'name_basics' in IMDB and 'actor' in Sakila, and the primary identifier is 'nconst' vs 'actor_id'.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into a single 'person' resource with 'person_id', merging both identity columns.

conflicts.description: The title/film entity is named 'title_basics' in IMDB and 'film' in Sakila; identifiers are 'tconst' vs 'film_id' and the headline title is 'primarytitle' vs 'title'.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into a 'title' resource with 'title_id' and 'primary_title'; source names retained only in source_provenance.

conflicts.description: Generic labels ('name', 'title', 'types') are reused for different concepts across the two schemas (category name, language name, alias title).
conflicts.resolution: Disambiguated by qualifying target field names (e.g. content_rating, content category 'name' vs alias 'title').

conflicts.description: 'film_text' replicates 'film' under a different name, representing the same entity (denormalized duplicate).
conflicts.resolution: Folded into the 'title' resource; its 'title' and 'description' columns contribute to the corresponding target fields.

conflicts.description: The actor-title relationship is named 'film_actor' in Sakila and 'title_principals' in IMDB for the same conceptual credit relationship.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into a single 'title_credit' resource.

conflicts.description: IMDB declares alphanumeric identifiers as 'number' while Sakila declares surrogate identifiers as 'string'; both are non-numeric keys.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized all identifiers (title_id, person_id, and all FK ids) to 'string'.

conflicts.description: 'primarytitle' is declared 'integer' although it holds a textual title (source mis-typing).
conflicts.resolution: Re-typed to 'string' in 'title.primary_title'.

conflicts.description: All year attributes are stored as 'string' (YYYY) in the sources.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized to 'integer' years (birth_year, death_year, start_year, end_year).

conflicts.description: Runtime is declared 'string' in Sakila but 'integer' in IMDB.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized to the integer field 'runtime_minutes'.

conflicts.description: Monetary and duration quantities are declared as 'string' although they are numeric.
conflicts.resolution: Re-typed to 'number' (rental_rate, replacement_cost, amount) and 'integer' (rental_duration).

conflicts.description: Boolean semantics are encoded as 'string' in Sakila (active) but as 'boolean' in IMDB (isadult, isoriginaltitle).
conflicts.resolution: Standardized to 'boolean' for all flags (active, is_adult, is_original_title).

conflicts.description: Temporal columns carrying a time component are declared as 'date'.
conflicts.resolution: Promoted to 'datetime' (rental_date, return_date, payment_date); pure calendar columns remain 'date'.

conflicts.description: Both are labelled 'rating' but represent different semantics: a 0–10 weighted numeric average vs an MPAA categorical rating (G/PG/PG-13/R/NC-17).
conflicts.resolution: Kept as separate fields, 'average_rating' (number) and 'content_rating' (string); no cross-mapping performed.

conflicts.description: 'genres' (IMDB) and 'category' (Sakila) are both title classifications but use different, non-identical vocabularies.
conflicts.resolution: Kept as distinct structures ('title_genre' string list vs 'category'/'title_category' dimension) rather than merged into one taxonomy.

conflicts.description: Language is represented as a free-text name/code in IMDB's alias table but as a normalized dimension reference in Sakila.
conflicts.resolution: Preserved distinctly: 'title_alias.language' stays a string attribute while Sakila languages become the 'language' dimension referenced by title FKs.

conflicts.description: Two different durations coexist (runtime in minutes vs rental period in days) and could be confused.
conflicts.resolution: Materialized as separate atomic fields 'runtime_minutes' and 'rental_duration' with distinct units/meaning.

conflicts.description: Sakila's actor link implies a fixed role ('actor') whereas IMDB's principals encode an explicit category/job attribute.
conflicts.resolution: Unified rows carry an optional 'category'; actor-only rows leave known-role attributes null without inventing derived categorical values.

conflicts.description: IMDB embeds array/multi-value attributes inside single columns, whereas Sakila normalizes relationships into separate tables.
conflicts.resolution: Multi-valued relationships were normalized into bridge tables (person_known_for, title_genre, title_director, title_writer, title_credit); free-text attribute arrays (types, attributes, characters, primary_profession) are retained as string fields.

conflicts.description: Sakila uses dedicated bridge tables for film-actor and film-category many-to-many structures.
conflicts.resolution: film_actor was merged into the unified 'title_credit' bridge; film_category maps to the 'title_category' bridge, preserving the normalized design.

conflicts.description: 'film_text' duplicates 'film' columns (film_id, title, description) creating redundancy and potential inconsistency.
conflicts.resolution: Removed as a duplicate; its columns were absorbed into the 'title' resource as additional provenance.

conflicts.description: Sakila separates person-like data into actor, customer and staff tables whereas IMDB keeps a single person table.
conflicts.resolution: 'actor' was merged with 'name_basics' into 'person'; 'customer' and 'staff' were retained as distinct entities because they model separate business roles with their own attributes.

conflicts.description: Title–person involvement is modeled with conflicting cardinality representations: title_crew stores arrays on a 1:1 title row while title_principals uses N rows per title.
conflicts.resolution: Both were decomposed into N:M bridge tables (title_director, title_writer, title_credit) so every relationship is many-to-many at the same grain.

conflicts.description: Three separate N:M title–person relationships (cast, principals, known-for) overlap conceptually.
conflicts.resolution: Cast and principals were merged into 'title_credit'; known-for remains a distinct relationship in 'person_known_for'.

conflicts.description: A self-referential series→episode hierarchy (1:N) exists in IMDB only.
conflicts.resolution: Modeled as 'title_episode' with parent_title_id and title_id both referencing the 'title' resource.

conflicts.description: Title-to-classification is N:M in Sakila (via bridge) but embedded 1:many inside a single IMDB column.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized the Sakila side as a bridge ('title_category') and the IMDB side as a comparable bridge ('title_genre').

conflicts.description: Sakila relates titles to a language dimension (N:1, twice) while IMDB carries language as a per-alias string.
conflicts.resolution: Foreign-key relationships (language_id, original_language_id) preserved for Sakila; the alias-level language string retained separately.

conflicts.description: Several source tables declare no primary key even though natural keys exist (e.g. title_akas: titleid+ordering; title_ratings: tconst; payment: payment_id).
conflicts.resolution: Inferred natural/composite keys and declared them as target primaryKeys ([title_id, ordering], title_id, [title_id, person_id], etc.).

conflicts.description: IMDB uses natural alphanumeric business keys while Sakila uses surrogate numeric keys; key types also differ (number vs string).
conflicts.resolution: Cross-source surrogate keys (title_id, person_id) unify the two key schemes, and both source keys are recorded in source_provenance.

conflicts.description: Two foreign keys in title_episode point to the same referenced entity (title_basics), a role-distinguished duplicate key situation.
conflicts.resolution: Both mapped to the same 'title' resource via distinct role-named columns (title_id and parent_title_id).

conflicts.description: film_text.film_id is a duplicated key of film.film_id with no declared PK or FK.
conflicts.resolution: Merged into the single 'title_id' key of the 'title' resource, eliminating the duplicate key.

conflicts.description: Foreign keys of different entity types (person vs title) risk being conflated across the merged bridge tables.
conflicts.resolution: Kept foreign keys semantically isolated: person identifiers only ever map to person_id (person), title identifiers only to title_id (title).

conflicts.description: The same real-world concept (an audiovisual work / motion picture) is named 'title_basics' in IMDb and 'film' in Sakila. The word 'title' is also overloaded in IMDb (title_basics.primarytitle, title_akas.title).
conflicts.resolution: Both entities are unified into a single resource named 'title'; the term 'title' is reserved for the work entity, its display name is renamed 'primary_title', and alternative-titles are renamed 'alternative_title'.

conflicts.description: The person entity is named 'name_basics' in IMDb and 'actor' in Sakila, though both represent individuals involved in productions.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into a single resource named 'person'.

conflicts.description: Homonym: 'category' denotes the job/role of a credited person in IMDb, but a film genre lookup table in Sakila.
conflicts.resolution: The IMDb concept is kept as the 'category' (role) column of 'title_credit'; the Sakila lookup is renamed and modeled as the 'genre' resource.

conflicts.description: Generic name columns ('name', 'city', 'country') are used to store the descriptive label of different lookups, causing name collisions across dimensions.
conflicts.resolution: Renamed to explicit, entity-qualified names: genre_name, language_name, city_name, country_name.

conflicts.description: The column name 'title' refers to four different things: the primary title, the localized alternative title, and (twice) the film title in two Sakila tables.
conflicts.resolution: Disambiguated into 'primary_title' (unified IMDb primarytitle + Sakila film/title_text title) and 'alternative_title' (IMDb title_akas title).

conflicts.description: The language concept is represented as an inline string column in IMDb and as an independent lookup table in Sakila.
conflicts.resolution: Modeled as a shared 'language' dimension; IMDb's per-alt-title language is captured via a language_id foreign key.

conflicts.description: 'film_text' duplicates the film title and description under a different name.
conflicts.resolution: Recognized as a denormalized copy of 'film'; merged into 'title' and not materialized as a separate resource.

conflicts.description: 'region' (IMDb) and 'country' (Sakila) both denominate geographic areas but with different labelling and granularity.
conflicts.resolution: Kept distinct: 'region' remains a title-distribution attribute on 'title_alternative'; 'country' is modeled as a normalized dimension.

conflicts.description: IMDb identifier columns are declared as 'number' although their descriptions state they are alphanumeric strings (e.g. 'tt0000001', 'nm0000001').
conflicts.resolution: Re-typed to 'string' across all target resources.

conflicts.description: Year values are declared as 'string' (YYYY) in IMDb and as 'string' in Sakila even though they are numeric.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized to 'integer' (birth_year, death_year, release_year, end_year).

conflicts.description: Declared as 'integer' although the description states it is the primary title string.
conflicts.resolution: Corrected to 'string' (primary_title).

conflicts.description: Sakila foreign-key columns are typed inconsistently: some 'integer' (film.language_id, address.city_id, inventory.film_id) while the referenced primary keys are 'string'.
conflicts.resolution: All identifier and foreign-key columns are uniformly typed as 'string'.

conflicts.description: Numeric measurements and money values are stored as 'string' in Sakila.
conflicts.resolution: Re-typed to 'integer' (rental_duration_days) and 'number' (rental_rate, replacement_cost, amount, runtime_minutes).

conflicts.description: Boolean flags are inconsistently typed: 'string' in Sakila (active) versus 'boolean' in IMDb (isadult, isoriginaltitle), and encoded as 0/1 in IMDb.
conflicts.resolution: All flags are typed 'boolean' (active, is_adult, is_original_title).

conflicts.description: Columns described as 'date and time' are typed 'date', losing the time component.
conflicts.resolution: Re-typed to 'datetime'.

conflicts.description: Sakila surrogate keys are declared as 'string' although they are integer surrogates, whereas IMDb uses alphanumeric natural keys.
conflicts.resolution: Uniformly typed 'string' to allow the merged keys of both sources to co-exist.

conflicts.description: Two different notions of 'rating': IMDb is a continuous weighted average (0-10), Sakila is a categorical age/MPAA rating (G, PG, PG-13, R, NC-17). Different scale and encoding.
conflicts.resolution: Kept as separate semantics: 'average_rating' (number) in the title_rating resource and 'content_rating' (string) on 'title'.

conflicts.description: Both express the runtime, and both use minutes as the unit; Sakila's column is however typed as string and unlabelled.
conflicts.resolution: Aligned on the common SI-friendly unit of minutes into a single 'runtime_minutes' integer column.

conflicts.description: IMDb encodes missing values with the literal '\N' inside year strings, which is a value-level encoding not representable once years become integers.
conflicts.resolution: The '\N' sentinel is normalized to a null value when casting years to integer.

conflicts.description: Same concept (language) encoded differently: IMDb uses ISO-like codes, Sakila uses English language names.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into a 'language' dimension; IMDb codes are harmonized to the dimension's identity while its name attribute carries the English label.

conflicts.description: Genre/category vocabularies differ between sources (IMDb's fixed genre set vs Sakila's rental-shop categories), and IMDb limits a title to three genres.
conflicts.resolution: Both are mapped into a single 'genre' dimension and a shared 'title_genre' bridge; vocabulary harmonization is left to a controlled value list.

conflicts.description: Active flags are documented to be set to 'FALSE' (rather than deleting rows), implying string/boolean ambiguity in encoding.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized to a real boolean type with a uniform true/false semantics.

conflicts.description: Geographic scope is represented at different granularities (distribution region, country dimension, and free-text district).
conflicts.resolution: Preserved as separate attributes at the correct granularity rather than forcing a lossy merge.

conflicts.description: IMDb stores many-to-many data as delimited/array values packed into a single column, whereas Sakila stores the same kinds of associations in fully normalized bridge tables.
conflicts.resolution: IMDb arrays are decomposed into bridge/child resources (title_genre, title_credit, person_profession, person_known_for) consistent with the normalized Sakila pattern; free-text arrays that are non-enumerated (attributes, types, characters) remain delimited strings.

conflicts.description: film_text is a denormalized projection of the film table (title + description keyed by film_id), introducing redundancy.
conflicts.resolution: Dropped as a separate resource; its columns are folded into 'title' with provenance retained.

conflicts.description: IMDb splits the title/person relationship across two tables of differing shape: title_crew packs director and writer arrays into one row per title, while title_principals holds one row per person credit.
conflicts.resolution: Both are unpivoted and unified into the row-per-credit 'title_credit' resource alongside Sakila's film_actor.

conflicts.description: Sakila has a normalized three-level location hierarchy that has no counterpart in IMDb.
conflicts.resolution: Preserved as separate country, city, and address resources, with foreign keys maintaining the hierarchy.

conflicts.description: IMDb models the series/episode relationship as a self-referencing association within a title-oriented table, unlike the flat Sakila model.
conflicts.resolution: Extracted into a dedicated 'title_episode' child resource with a self-referencing foreign key to 'title'.

conflicts.description: Sakila contains a complete rental/commerce domain (inventory, rental, payment, store, staff, customer) with no counterpart in IMDb.
conflicts.resolution: Retained as-is (normalized to the unified 'title' foreign key where it referenced 'film'), as these are legitimate domain-specific resources.

conflicts.description: The title-to-ratings relationship is 1:1 (a single ratings row per title), whereas most other audio-visual relationships are 1:N or N:M.
conflicts.resolution: Modeled as a 1:1 extension resource 'title_rating' whose primary key is the title_id foreign key.

conflicts.description: Person-to-title is N:M in both sources but is expressed through different mechanisms and role semantics.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into the N:M 'title_credit' bridge between 'person' and 'title'.

conflicts.description: Sakila title-to-genre is a clean N:M bridge; IMDb embeds an inline array of up to three genres per title.
conflicts.resolution: Unified into the N:M 'title_genre' bridge.

conflicts.description: A TV series relates 1:N to its episodes, and each episode maps back to exactly one parent series.
conflicts.resolution: Represented via self-referencing foreign keys on 'title_episode'.

conflicts.description: Circular 1:N references between store and staff (a store has a manager staff member; a staff member belongs to a home store).
conflicts.resolution: Both foreign keys are retained in the unified schema; the cycle is preserved as-is.

conflicts.description: The 'known for' relationship is 1:N from a person to several titles in IMDb.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized into the 'person_known_for' resource linking person to title.

conflicts.description: title_akas declares no primary key, although the pair (titleid, ordering) is the natural unique identifier.
conflicts.resolution: Adopted the composite natural key (title_id, ordering) as the primary key of 'title_alternative'.

conflicts.description: Several IMDb tables declare no primary key at all, despite having natural keys (tconst, or tconst+ordering).
conflicts.resolution: Natural keys are inferred: title_episode and title_rating use title_id; title_credit uses a synthetic surrogate key because its natural key spans unpivoted sources.

conflicts.description: Primary-key conventions differ: IMDb uses alphanumeric natural keys (typed as number) while Sakila uses integer surrogate keys (typed as string).
conflicts.resolution: Both key styles are unified as 'string' identifiers, and merged entities reuse them (title_id, person_id).

conflicts.description: Sakila bridge tables declare no primary key even though (film_id, actor_id) and (film_id, category_id) are unique.
conflicts.resolution: Composite primary keys are declared on the corresponding bridge resources (title_genre; title_credit exposed via a surrogate key).

conflicts.description: payment declares payment_id but does not mark it as the primary key, while rental does mark rental_id.
conflicts.resolution: payment_id is adopted as the primary key of 'payment'.

conflicts.description: Merging entities from two independent sources produces several source primary keys feeding one target key.
conflicts.resolution: The unified 'person' and 'title' primary keys list all contributing source primary keys in their provenance.

conflicts.description: Synthea uses plural entity naming conventions (e.g., 'patients', 'encounters', 'conditions', 'medications', 'providers', 'organizations') whereas OMOP CDM uses singular conventions (e.g., 'person', 'visit_occurrence', 'condition_occurrence', 'drug_exposure', 'provider', 'care_site').
conflicts.resolution: Adopted canonical, standardized OMOP naming conventions across merged clinical resources (e.g., 'person', 'provider', 'care_site', 'visit_occurrence', 'condition_occurrence', 'drug_exposure', 'procedure_occurrence', 'measurement', 'observation').

conflicts.description: Synthea names encounter identifiers and foreign keys as 'encounter' and 'patient', whereas OMOP uses 'visit_occurrence_id' and 'person_id'.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized on OMOP relational key naming conventions ('person_id', 'visit_occurrence_id', 'provider_id', 'care_site_id').

conflicts.description: Imaging studies body site, modality, and SOP fields contain spaces in Synthea ('body site code', 'modality code', etc.).
conflicts.resolution: Normalized column identifiers into clean snake_case attributes.

conflicts.description: Synthea financial cost fields ('cost' in encounters, immunizations, medications, procedures) are defined as 'string', whereas OMOP cost amounts and financial metrics are represented as numbers/floats or stored in dedicated cost entities.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized financial and cost fields to numeric 'number' generic frictionless data types.

conflicts.description: OMOP vocabulary_name is typed as 'integer' and payer_plan_period_id as 'date' in the OMOP source schema, while conceptually representing string/alphanumeric identifiers and names. Similarly Synthea observation type is 'number' while representing a string concept/datatype description.
conflicts.resolution: Reconciled all identifier and name types to generic frictionless 'string'.

conflicts.description: Synthea start and stop fields are defined as 'date', while OMOP provides both 'date' and precise 'datetime' representations.
conflicts.resolution: Supported standardized date and datetime types, mapping source dates to start_date and stop_date.

conflicts.description: Synthea stores clinical diagnoses, procedures, and medications as direct coding system values (e.g. SNOMED-CT, RxNorm, CVX codes and text descriptions), whereas OMOP utilizes standardized concept identifiers (e.g., concept_id) paired with source value tracking columns (e.g., source_value, source_concept_id).
conflicts.resolution: Unified coding attributes by aligning Synthea codes and descriptions into OMOP source value fields and concept reference fields.

conflicts.description: Gender is recorded as single-character codes ('m', 'f') in Synthea, whereas OMOP supports standard concept IDs along with source values.
conflicts.resolution: Mapped Synthea gender to gender_source_value and supported gender_concept_id.

conflicts.description: In Synthea, patient address components (address, city, state, zip) are embedded directly within the 'patients', 'providers', and 'organizations' tables, whereas OMOP normalizes address attributes into a distinct 'location' table.
conflicts.resolution: Integrated the normalized 'location' resource to encapsulate spatial addresses, referencing it via location_id across person, care_site, and provider entities while retaining source mapping provenance.

conflicts.description: Synthea captures death information directly on the 'patients' table via 'deathdate', whereas OMOP normalizes patient death events into a dedicated 'death' table.
conflicts.resolution: Maintained the dedicated 'death' table and linked Synthea's deathdate to OMOP death_date.

conflicts.description: Synthea includes allergy diagnoses and imaging studies which OMOP typically maps into observation, condition_occurrence, or measurement domains.
conflicts.resolution: Retained dedicated resources for imaging studies and care plans while fully integrating clinical observations, procedures, and drug exposures.

conflicts.description: Synthea models clinical encounters as a single-level table with base costs and reason codes, whereas OMOP accommodates both summary encounters ('visit_occurrence') and sub-encounters ('visit_detail').
conflicts.resolution: Aligned Synthea encounters to OMOP 'visit_occurrence' as the primary visit entity and preserved 'visit_detail' for granular service unit breakdowns.

conflicts.description: Synthea tables frequently omit primary key definitions (e.g., conditions, allergies, immunizations, procedures, observations have null primary keys), whereas OMOP specifies explicit unique identifiers.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized primary keys across all unified tables using canonical identifier fields (e.g., condition_occurrence_id, procedure_occurrence_id, measurement_id, observation_id, person_id, visit_occurrence_id).

conflicts.description: Entity and attribute naming differences between Synthea patient-centric naming (e.g. 'patients.birthdate', 'encounters', 'procedures') and OMOP CDM standardized relational naming (e.g. 'person.birth_datetime', 'visit_occurrence', 'procedure_occurrence').
conflicts.resolution: Harmonized domain entities onto OMOP-aligned standardized snake_case schema naming conventions, mapping Synthea entities directly into the unified resources.

conflicts.description: Attribute naming discrepancies for organizational entities: Synthea uses 'organizations' with columns 'address', 'city', 'state', 'zip' whereas OMOP uses 'care_site' joined to 'location' and 'provider'.
conflicts.resolution: Preserved unified care site/organization resource capturing core administrative and geographic attributes.

conflicts.description: Cost fields in Synthea (e.g. 'encounters.cost', 'procedures.cost', 'immunizations.cost') are represented as strings, whereas monetary amounts are quantitative numbers.
conflicts.resolution: Standardized financial/cost fields to Frictionless generic type 'number'.

conflicts.description: Observation value types differ: Synthea stores 'value' as string with a numeric 'type' flag, while OMOP supports both 'value_as_number' (number) and 'value_as_string' (string).
conflicts.resolution: Standardized distinct columns for string and numeric observation values.

conflicts.description: Synthea stores addresses embedded directly within entity records ('patients', 'organizations', 'providers'), while OMOP normalizes geographic addresses into a dedicated 'location' table.
conflicts.resolution: Normalized address attributes into a shared location structure and preserved foreign key relationships referencing location across persons, providers, and care sites.

conflicts.description: Synthea represents allergies, care plans, and immunizations as dedicated clinical event tables, whereas OMOP standardizes these as clinical events across condition_occurrence, drug_exposure, observation, and procedure_occurrence.
conflicts.resolution: Maintained explicit normalized tables for clinical domains while capturing OMOP-aligned concepts, occurrence intervals, and source mappings.

conflicts.description: Synthea encodes clinical conditions and procedures primarily using SNOMED-CT text codes directly, whereas OMOP relies on mapped standard concept IDs alongside source concept IDs and verbatim source values.
conflicts.resolution: Modeled both standard concept identifiers and verbatim/source codes and descriptions to support dual semantic representations without information loss.

conflicts.description: Synthea clinical tables lack explicit primary keys in schema definition, relying on implicit event instances, whereas OMOP defines unique primary keys for every event occurrence (e.g., 'condition_occurrence_id', 'procedure_occurrence_id').
conflicts.resolution: Defined surrogate primary keys for all target event entities and mapped source identifiers where available.

conflicts.description: Discrepancy in table and field naming conventions between Synthea and OMOP (e.g. Synthea 'patients' vs OMOP 'person', Synthea 'encounters' vs OMOP 'visit_occurrence', Synthea 'conditions' vs OMOP 'condition_occurrence', Synthea 'medications' vs OMOP 'drug_exposure', Synthea 'observations' vs OMOP 'measurement'/'observation', Synthea 'organizations' vs OMOP 'care_site').
conflicts.resolution: Standardized to standard snake_case canonical clinical domain models aligned with OMOP Common Data Model terminology and structure.

conflicts.description: Field naming differences for identical clinical concepts (e.g., patient identifier 'patient' vs 'person_id', provider identifier 'provider' vs 'provider_id', encounter identifier 'encounter' vs 'visit_occurrence_id').
conflicts.resolution: Adopted canonical snake_case field identifiers (e.g., 'person_id', 'provider_id', 'visit_occurrence_id').

conflicts.description: Synthea models cost fields ('cost') and utilization counts as strings, whereas OMOP represents costs in the 'cost' table with numerical representations or strings, and vocabulary_name as an integer in OMOP metadata.
conflicts.resolution: Harmonized financial and quantity amounts to numeric types (number) and names/identifiers to appropriate string types.

conflicts.description: Synthea observation 'value' is string while OMOP splits into 'value_as_number' (number) and 'value_as_string' (string).
conflicts.resolution: Retained distinct value type fields (value_as_number, value_as_string, and value_as_concept_id) to accurately support both continuous and categorical results.

conflicts.description: Synthea stores medical concepts as source vocabulary code strings (e.g., SNOMED, RxNorm, CVX, LOINC) accompanied by text descriptions directly in the event tables, whereas OMOP maps clinical events to standardized integer Concept IDs and retains source values in dedicated source value columns.
conflicts.resolution: Included both concept ID foreign keys for standardized terminology mapping and source value/code string fields with explicit provenance mapping to the Synthea source codes.

conflicts.description: Synthea embeds geographic address attributes (street address, city, state, zip) directly within patient, provider, and organization records, whereas OMOP normalizes geographic location details into a separate 'location' table referenced via 'location_id'.
conflicts.resolution: Unified address attributes into a normalized 'location' resource and linked person, provider, and care_site entities to it via 'location_id'.

conflicts.description: Synthea models financial costs as embedded columns inside clinical event records (encounters, medications, immunizations, procedures), whereas OMOP consolidates costs into an independent 'cost' table.
conflicts.resolution: Retained a consolidated 'cost' resource capable of referencing any domain event through domain and event foreign identifiers, while also supporting direct event association.

conflicts.description: Synthea captures allergies, conditions, medications, procedures, and imaging studies as direct 1:N relations with encounter and patient, whereas OMOP supports micro-level hierarchies (e.g. visit_occurrence to visit_detail) and composite episode groupings.
conflicts.resolution: Structured target entities to support both direct visit/encounter linking and extended visit_detail/episode associations without loss of granularity.

conflicts.description: Synthea tables like allergies, immunizations, conditions, and procedures lack explicit primary key designations in schema definitions, whereas OMOP standardizes surrogate event primary keys (e.g. condition_occurrence_id, procedure_occurrence_id).
conflicts.resolution: Designated canonical primary keys across all unified target entity tables with synthetic keys where missing in source records.
